subChunks.title: How Indexes Work and When to Create Them
subChunks.hookHtml: A query that takes 5 seconds on 1 million rows can take 1 millisecond with the right index. Understanding how indexes work explains when they help and when they don't.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What an index is

An index is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations. Without an index, finding rows with WHERE email = 'alice@example.com' requires scanning every row. With an index on email, the engine jumps directly to matching rows in O(log n).

Creating an index

-- Single column:
CREATE INDEX idx_apprentices_rank ON apprentices (rank);

-- Unique index (also enforces uniqueness):
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_apprentices_email ON apprentices (email);

-- Dropping:
DROP INDEX idx_apprentices_rank;

When indexes help

  • Equality filters: WHERE rank = 'Mage'
  • Range filters: WHERE xp BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000
  • JOIN conditions: ON a.mentor_id = m.id — foreign key columns are almost always worth indexing
  • ORDER BY on large tables (index can provide pre-sorted order)

When indexes hurt

  • High-write tables: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update the index
  • Low-selectivity columns: indexing a boolean column with only 2 values is rarely useful
  • Functions applied to the column: WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE' cannot use an index on name

Selectivity

A column is highly selective if most values are distinct (e.g. email). Low-selectivity columns (e.g. a boolean or a status with 3 values) benefit less from indexing.

storyBeats.text: The apprentice search page now has a million records. Queries that took milliseconds take seconds.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: An index is a shortcut. The B-tree sorts and maps values to rows — like the index at the back of a book. Without it the engine reads every page; with it, it jumps directly. But every shortcut has a cost: each INSERT maintains the index. Index the columns you filter and join on; do not index everything.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Index design exercise

Given these queries, identify which columns should be indexed and explain your reasoning:

Q1: SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE email = $1;
Q2: SELECT * FROM apprentices ORDER BY xp DESC LIMIT 10;
Q3: SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE is_active = TRUE;
Q4: SELECT * FROM quest_completions WHERE apprentice_id = $1;
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Q1: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON apprentices(email) — email is high-selectivity (nearly every row distinct) and queried frequently. UNIQUE also enforces data integrity.

Q2: CREATE INDEX ON apprentices(xp DESC) — the ORDER BY xp DESC can use this index to avoid a sort. Without it, the engine sorts all rows before taking 10.

Q3: No index recommended — is_active is a boolean with only 2 values (low selectivity). The engine would read ~50% of rows regardless; a full scan may be cheaper than index overhead.

Q4: CREATE INDEX ON quest_completions(apprentice_id) — foreign key columns used in JOINs and WHERE filters are the most critical indexes to add. This is almost always missing and is the biggest JOIN performance win.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain why `WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE'` cannot use a standard index on name, and describe two alternatives that would allow index use.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A standard B-tree index on `name` stores the original values ('Alice', 'Bjorn'...). When the engine evaluates `UPPER(name)`, it must call UPPER on every row — it cannot use the index because the indexed value and the compared value are in different forms.

Alternative 1: Store names in uppercase at insertion time and query with `WHERE name = 'ALICE'`. The index on name now matches.

Alternative 2: Create a functional/expression index: `CREATE INDEX ON apprentices (UPPER(name))`. PostgreSQL supports this. The index maps UPPER(name) values, so `WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ALICE'` can use it.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a B-tree index is, why it makes equality queries faster, and why adding indexes to every column is not a good idea.

questions.prompt: What data structure does a standard SQL index use?
questions.explanation: Standard SQL indexes use B-tree (balanced tree) structures. B-trees support equality, range (BETWEEN), and order queries in O(log n). Hash indexes support only equality queries but are faster for them (available as an option in PostgreSQL).

questions.prompt: A table has 10 million rows. Which column benefits most from an index?
options: country_code (200 distinct values out of 10M rows)
created_at (only queried in GROUP BY reports)
questions.explanation: Selectivity = (distinct values) / (total rows). Email is ~1.0 selectivity — nearly every row is unique. An index on a unique column reduces a full scan to O(log n). Low-selectivity columns (boolean, small enum) give less benefit because the engine still reads a large fraction of rows.

questions.prompt: Why should foreign key columns almost always be indexed?
options: JOIN and WHERE conditions on foreign keys are very common — without an index, every JOIN requires a full scan of the child table
Foreign key constraints require an index to function
Indexes on foreign keys are created automatically
Foreign keys must be unique, requiring a UNIQUE index
questions.answer: JOIN and WHERE conditions on foreign keys are very common — without an index, every JOIN requires a full scan of the child table
questions.explanation: Foreign key columns appear in ON conditions of JOINs constantly. Without an index, the engine scans the entire child table for each parent row. The missing FK index is one of the most common performance mistakes in schema design.

questions.prompt: Why can adding too many indexes to a write-heavy table be harmful?
options: Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must also update each index — more indexes = more write overhead per row modification
Indexes use storage that could be used for data
The query planner becomes confused by too many index choices
questions.answer: Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must also update each index — more indexes = more write overhead per row modification
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but slow writes. Each write operation must maintain every index on the table. A table with 10 indexes on a 10M-row high-insert workload can have significantly higher write latency than the same table with 2 targeted indexes.
